sense: see to it that something happens

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation: ut or nē and the subjunctive
terms.comment: The everyday way, in speech and in letters: cūrā ut valeās, “see that you keep well”, is how Cicero ends a letter. Its first sense is “look after, take care of” (cūrāre corpus), and with an accusative and a gerundive it is “have something done” (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation: in this sense with ut or nē and the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.1.2: nāvem idōneam ut habeās, dīligenter vidēbis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Mostly as a request or an order: vidē ut, vidēbis ut, videndum est ut. Vidē nē is also a warning, “mind you don’t …”, and vidē quid agās “think what you are doing”.

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō): ut and the subjunctive
terms.comment: When the result takes work or contrivance; its general sense is “cause, bring about” (see cause).
